ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Two metal rails are placed parallel to each other on the same horizontal plane, separated by a distance of $l = 0.6 \, \mathrm{m}$. The left and right ends of the rails are connected to lamps $\mathrm{L}_{1}$ and $\mathrm{L}_{2}$ with specifications "3V, 3W" and "6V, 6W" respectively. A conductor rod ab with resistance $\mathbf{r} = 1 \, \Omega$ is placed on the rails and is perpendicular to them. A uniform magnetic field with magnetic induction $\mathrm{B} = 1 \, \mathrm{T}$ passes vertically through the plane of the rails. When the conductor rod moves to the right at a constant speed under the action of an external force, lamp $\mathrm{L}_{1}$ just lights up normally. The resistance of the rails is negligible.

1. The actual power $\mathrm{P}_{2}$ of the lamp $\mathrm{L}_{2}$.
2. The speed $v$ of the conductor rod $ab$.
3. The power of the Ampere force acting on the conductor rod ab $\mathrm{P_{Ampere}}$.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure there are two upper and lower parallel metal rails, the left end is connected to bulb L1, and the right end is connected to bulb L2; a vertical conducting rod ab is bridged between the upper and lower rails and is perpendicular to the rails. In the figure, on the right side of the conducting rod there is a velocity arrow v pointing to the right, and the magnetic field region is represented by “×”, indicating that the magnetic field is perpendicular to the paper surface inward. Since the resistance of the upper and lower rails can be neglected, L1, L2, and the conducting-rod branch are all connected between the same pair of ideal upper and lower rails, and can be regarded as parallel. Reasoning calculation: The specification of bulb L1 is “3 V, 3 W”, so its resistance R1 = U1^2/P1 = 3^2/3 = 3 Ω. The specification of bulb L2 is “6 V, 6 W”, so its resistance R2 = U2^2/P2 rated = 6^2/6 = 6 Ω. L1 just emits light normally, therefore the voltage across the two ends of the rails is U = 3 V, and the current flowing through L1 is I1 = U/R1 = 3/3 = 1 A. L2 is in parallel with L1, and the terminal voltage is likewise 3 V, so the actual power of L2 is P2 = U^2/R2 = 3^2/6 = 1.5 W, and the current flowing through L2 is I2 = U/R2 = 3/6 = 0.5 A. From the node current relation, the current provided by the conducting-rod branch is I = I1 + I2 = 1 + 0.5 = 1.5 A. Treat the moving conducting rod as a power source with electromotive force E and internal resistance r = 1 Ω; its terminal voltage is U = 3 V, therefore E = U + Ir = 3 + 1.5 × 1 = 4.5 V. The induced electromotive force generated by the moving conducting rod is E = Blv, so v = E/(Bl) = 4.5/(1 × 0.6) = 7.5 m/s. The magnitude of the power of the Ampere force is P_Ampere = BIlv = 1 × 1.5 × 0.6 × 7.5 = 6.75 W. If according to the sign of the work done by the force on the conducting rod, the direction of the Ampere force is opposite to the velocity, and the power is negative; the standard result of this problem takes the magnitude.
